summary:
Guadeloupe stands under France's national framework. French criminal law, the anti-discrimination statute, the marriage regime and the rules on identity documents apply here as they do in the metropole. Same-sex relations were decriminalised in the Penal Code of 1791 and retained in the 1810 Code, though public morality provisions were subsequently used against LGBTQ people. No legal penalty attaches to trans existence.

Legal gender recognition follows the simplified French procedure, available since 1 January 2017 under a law signed on 18 November 2016. Surgery and medical diagnosis are no longer required, and both self-certification of gender and proof of medical treatment were dropped from the final bill. A change of first name is handled at the registry office; a change of the gender marker still requires an appearance before a court. A 2017 bid to have the law recognise a 'neutral sex' classification was rejected by the Court of Cassation.

Placement in detention follows the legal gender recorded on the person's incarceration papers, which may not correspond to how the person presents. Reporting from January 2018 indicates that in practice assignment weighs the individual's best interests, with individual cells or placement in more welcoming wings used as accommodations. The national detention-oversight body, the CGLPL, issued an opinion on 25 May 2021 finding that serious violations of fundamental rights of transgender people persist across places of deprivation of liberty, drawing on some 40 referrals since 2010.

Protection against hostility rests on the law of 31 December 2004, which made homophobic, sexist, racist and xenophobic comments punishable by a fine of up to €45,000 and 12 months' imprisonment and amended the 1881 Freedom of the Press Law to cover incitement to hatred or violence or discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation. A conversion therapy ban passed the Senate on 7 December 2020 and was published on 1 February 2022, carrying two years' imprisonment and/or a €30,000 fine. A report released on 16 May 2020 recorded homophobic and transphobic attacks and insults rising 36% in 2019, with police identifying around 1,870 victims against about 1,380 in 2018.

Gender-affirming care is legal domestically since 1979 and funded through the Sécurité Sociale under the ALD 31 long-term illness provision; France declassified gender dysphoria as a mental illness by decree in 2010, a step French trans rights organisations said changed little in practice. A 2022 ILGA-Europe report found significant problems in gender-affirming healthcare, citing lack of self-determination, extended waiting times and inequitable access depending on location, and recommended an informed-consent model. In late 2024 the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology issued the country's first trans youth guidelines, recommending puberty blockers from Tanner stage 2. A bill to ban medical transition under 18 passed the Senate in May 2024, opposed by the Macron government, and has had no recorded movement since 23 July 2024.

Support infrastructure on the island is thin but growing. The Maison des Diversités et de l'Inclusion, Guadeloupe's first LGBT+ centre, opened on 24 April 2024, offering reception, support and orientation for people of diverse identity, sexual, bodily and gender diversities, driven by a federation of Guadeloupean associations. Minister Aurore Bergé attended the opening and announced measures to strengthen the fight against gender-based violence and discrimination in Guadeloupe, with structures adapted for overseas territories.
tangentialFactors:
French legal history carries provisions that were used against LGBTQ people even without a sodomy statute on the books. In Alsace and Lorraine, annexed in 1940, men were interned in Nazi camps and persecuted under Vichy despite the absence of a sodomy law. Vichy's article 334 of 6 August 1942, later 331, set the age of consent for homosexual relations at 21 against 15 for heterosexual relations, lowered to 18 in 1974 and equalised at 15 on 4 August 1982. The Mirguet amendment of 1960 doubled penalties for indecent exposure in homosexual activity under article 330, 2nd alinea, and was repealed in 1980. In March 2024 the National Assembly unanimously passed a compensation bill for men arrested under article 330 before 1980; the Senate has yet to vote.

Official rhetoric on trans and gender-diverse people is contested rather than settled. The French Académie Nationale de Médecine characterised the rise in trans people seeking treatment as an 'epidemic-like phenomenon' and 'a primarily social problem', advising extreme caution on access, without changing actual practice. In March 2024 centre-right senators commissioned the Little Mermaid Observatory, a group opposed to all gender transition for minors, to report on youth gender care; it called transition a 'health scandal' and transness a 'social contagion'. In 2022 it emerged that the president of the scientific committee of DILCRAH, the interministerial body against racism, anti-Semitism and anti-LGBT hatred, was a member of that Observatory; one member resigned and the president stepped away.

Documentation of hostility is uneven. In October 2018 President Macron denounced homophobic violence as 'unworthy of France' after a rise in attacks. Large-scale protests followed the Senate's May 2024 passage of the under-18 transition ban. France's 2004 hate-speech law drew criticism from civil liberties groups including Reporters Without Borders as a serious infringement of free speech; Christian Vanneste, an MP from the ruling UMP party, became the first person convicted under it in January 2006, though that conviction was later cancelled by the Court of Cassation.

Guadeloupe's community organisations describe momentum rather than consolidation: local activists say LGBTQ people are increasingly reconciling their lives with their orientation, with activism advancing after the neighbouring island of Martinique, and three groups partnered on a year of LGBT-friendly social events across Guadeloupe in 2025.
localsOnly:
Recognition of parentage has shifted through the courts. The Court of Cassation ruled on 5 July 2017 that a child born to a surrogate abroad can be adopted by the partner of the biological father; the Court of Appeal of Paris held in May 2019 that a Canadian birth certificate must be recognised; and in December 2019 the Court of Cassation ruled that foreign birth certificates recognising same-sex partners must be fully recognised in France. In 2022 a court of appeal ruled that a transgender woman should be considered the mother of the child she conceived before her sex change. Until 2015 France refused to recognise surrogate children as French citizens, leaving many in legal limbo.

Students and staff in the education system have named routes. The Ministry of Education launched the campaign 'Tous égaux, tous alliés' in January 2019 to tackle anti-LGBTQ bullying, providing reporting services and a helpline for students and staff, and requiring all French schools to give guidance on LGBTQ issues with 17 May as a special sensitisation day; in March 2008 Education Minister Xavier Darcos had named fighting homophobia among 15 national education priorities for 2008–2009. In March 2019 Higher Education Minister Frédérique Vidal announced that all higher education institutions should use transgender people's preferred names, including on student cards and exam forms.

Local associations operate a sustained programme of activity. Secret's Out, Queer Gang and Lovo Nova are partnering on LGBT-friendly social events across Guadeloupe through 2025. Community organisers including Leïla of Secret's Out and Prisca Melyon-Reinette of Amalgame Humani's describe a widening space for openly living LGBTQ lives on the island. Guadeloupe's first LGBT+ centre provides a fixed point of contact for reception, support and orientation.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the Senate bill to ban medical transition for under-18s advanced after 23 July 2024 is unresolved in the sources available; the most recent record has no movement past that date.

The Senate vote on the March 2024 compensation bill for men arrested under article 330 before 1980 remains outstanding and is unresolved here.

Whether the 2019 figure of a 36% rise in homophobic and transphobic attacks is reported separately for Guadeloupe is not sourced; the national totals given do not break down by overseas department.

The CGLPL's 2021 opinion addresses places of deprivation of liberty in the French context generally; how far its findings apply specifically to detention facilities in Guadeloupe is not sourced.

Access to gender-affirming care in Guadeloupe itself, including waiting times and the availability of clinicians, is not sourced. The 2022 ILGA-Europe findings on inequitable access depending on location do not name this territory.

Whether the Maison des Diversités et de l'Inclusion receives sustained state funding, and what became of the measures announced by Aurore Bergé at its opening, is unresolved.
